title: Not Offending the Great
note: This is not living in contempt of the great, meaning both rulers, great in power, and sages, great in penance. It closes the chapters on what anger brings.

couplets.plain: Of all the ways to keep yourself safe, the first is not to scorn the power of those who can get things done.
couplets.pm: Not scorning the power of those able to finish whatever they take up is the highest of all the guards people keep against harm. Power means greatness, knowledge and effort. “Those who can” shows that, if scorned, they can remove you. Forts, armies, wealth and friends are all destroyed by them, so this is the chief guard.

links.quote: not to scorn the power of those who can get things done
those who can get things done
links.reason: Sets those who can get things done apart as the ones above all not to scorn.

couplets.plain: Live without respect for the great, and it will bring you lasting pain through the great.
couplets.pm: If rulers carry on in contempt of those great in power, that conduct brings them, through those great ones, pains that never leave. These are the three kinds of pain, running without break through this life and the next. The conduct is named as the doer and the great as its tool, to show they bring it all on themselves.

links.reason: The great themselves are the means by which the pain comes.

couplets.plain: If you want your ruin, don’t listen: offend those who can kill the moment they wish.
couplets.pm: If someone wants to be ruined, let him go beyond statecraft and offend rulers who can kill other rulers the moment they wish. It says “don’t listen” because statecraft says this must not be done.
couplets.sensitive: Mock recipe for one's own destruction; risky read literally

links.quote: offend those who can kill the moment they wish

links.reason: Refusing to listen is the first step in its mocking recipe for ruin.

couplets.plain: For the powerless to harm the powerful is like beckoning Death with your hand.
couplets.pm: When those without the three powers strike first at those who have them, it is like waving to Death, who would come anyway, to come sooner. Calling with the hand shows contempt. Those who could take their life in any case are hurried on to them, so their death is both certain and near.
couplets.sensitive: Warns the weak against standing up to the powerful.

links.quote: For the powerless to harm the powerful
links.reason: For the weak to harm the mighty is to invite their own end.

couplets.plain: Go where they may, those who draw the anger of a fiercely strong ruler will live nowhere.
couplets.pm: Rulers attacked by a ruler of fierce strength can’t escape him and live anywhere. No one shelters those who flee their land. Hosts kill them to win that ruler’s friendship and to seize the wealth that has come to their door, or else perish with them.

links.reason: Whoever draws a strong ruler’s anger finds no refuge anywhere.

couplets.plain: You may survive being burned by fire. Those who offend the great will not survive.
couplets.pm: Someone caught in a forest fire may somehow live. Those who offend men great in penance can’t live in any way. Fire takes the body first and reaches life through it, so you may escape midway. The anger of great ascetics lasts only a moment, yet in that moment no one can be saved. So don’t commit the offence that causes it.

links.quote: Those who offend the great will not survive

couplets.plain: What becomes of a splendid life and vast wealth, if the truly worthy turn in anger on you?
couplets.pm: If great ascetics, whose greatness can curse and bless, grow angry with a ruler, what is left of his kingdom, fine in every part, and his piled-up wealth? The parts are ministers, land, forts and army. “If” shows they don’t readily grow angry. If rulers, drunk on wealth, wrong such men, it all burns in a moment in that fire of anger.

links.quote: if the truly worthy turn in anger on you
links.reason: A splendid life and vast wealth count for nothing once the worthy turn in anger.

couplets.plain: When those who are like mountains wish someone’s fall, people who seemed fixed on the earth vanish, with their families.
couplets.pm: If great ascetics, who are like mountains, think of ruin, the rich who seem fixed on this earth perish at once with their families. The ascetics are like mountains in bearing sun and rain and in never wavering. The rich seem fixed because they are so great that onlookers think they can never fall.

links.reason: People who seem fixed on the earth vanish, with their families, at the mere will of the great.

couplets.plain: When those of lofty vows flare up, even a ruler breaks midway and loses his rule.
couplets.pm: If those who hold lofty vows, hard to keep, flare up, even the king of the gods loses his place midway by their power and falls. He has in mind the man who won that throne, grew drunk with joy on his way to it, angered a sage, and lost it midway under his curse.
couplets.note: வேந்தன் reads as any ruler. He takes it as the king of the gods.

links.quote: even a ruler breaks midway and loses his rule
links.reason: The anger of those with lofty vows is enough to unseat a ruler.
Places those of lofty vows above even a ruler.

couplets.plain: Even those with the greatest of supports won’t survive if those of surpassing worth turn on them in anger.
couplets.pm: If those of surpassing penance grow angry, those they are angry with won’t survive, however great their supports. Supports are forts, army, wealth and friends. The power of the angry one destroys them all, like the three cities of the old story.

links.quote: Even those with the greatest of supports won’t survive
links.reason: The greatest support gives no protection from the anger of those of surpassing worth.
